implementation_notes: With only the standard library, the repository is `mpsc::sync_channel(n)` - the bounded form, because `channel()` is unbounded and queues without limit - and the executor is one or more `thread::spawn`ed workers whose loop is `while let Ok(cmd) = rx.recv()`; recv returning `Err` *is* the shutdown protocol, since it means every sender was dropped. Commands are either a trait object (`Box<dyn Command + Send>`) or, more idiomatically, a plain enum matched in the worker, which keeps them `Send`, `Clone`-free and cheap. Ownership is why history/undo needs deliberate design: an executed command has moved into the worker, so a log stores a serialisable *description* (serde) plus an inverse rather than the command itself, and shared receiver state lives in an Arc<Mutex<_>>.
pitfalls: `mpsc::channel()` is unbounded: producers never block and an overloaded system grows until the allocator fails - use sync_channel with a capacity.
Only one consumer can own the Receiver; to fan out to several workers you need a mutex-guarded shared receiver or one channel per worker (or crossbeam/tokio primitives).
Commands crossing a thread boundary must be `Send`; an enum or Arc-based command is fine, a Box<dyn FnOnce()> holding Rc/&references is not.
A panicking worker thread is invisible unless the join handle is checked; the processor should catch_unwind or log from inside the loop.
For replay, the command enum must be serialisable and versioned; an enum that only exists in memory cannot be persisted.

variants.name: tokio::sync::mpsc + spawned tasks (async runtime)
variants.implementation_notes: On an async runtime the same roles are played by `tokio::sync::mpsc::channel(n)` (bounded; `send().await` suspends the producer when full) and one or more `tokio::spawn`ed tasks draining it, with `tokio::select!` for graceful shutdown and prioritised streams. Commands are async closures or a serde-serialisable enum; per-command results come back through a oneshot channel, which is the async analogue of the `Future` the blocking variant records. Prefer this variant when receivers are I/O-bound and a runtime is already present; prefer std threads when commands are CPU-bound or the runtime dependency is unwanted.
pitfalls: Holding a std::sync::MutexGuard across `.await` is a compile error for good reason - use tokio::sync::Mutex or scope the lock so it cannot span an await point.
spawned tasks detach: a panic inside one is swallowed unless the JoinHandle is awaited or the task is instrumented, so the processor must log failures itself.
The runtime must be shut down gracefully: dropping the runtime cancels spawned tasks mid-command, leaving state half-updated (drain with the sender dropped plus a JoinSet).
CPU-heavy commands must be moved off the async worker with spawn_blocking, or they stall the runtime's worker threads.
